title: Cutting Down the Tall Poppies? Social Disapproval, Emotional Trade-Offs and Family Agency in Non-Native Bilingual Parenting in Spain
content: Driven by neoliberal pressures and an intensive parenting ideal, a growing number of monolingual Spanish parents are raising their children in English, a language that is neither the community language nor their own mother tongue, a practice known as non-native bilingualism (NNB). This qualitative multiple-case study, drawn from a broader project with seventeen families, examines two middle-class families in cen-tral-southern Spain (Castilla-La Mancha): one that relies on a one-parent-one-language (OPOL) approach and one that relies mainly on external resources such as academies, language camps and a stay abroad. Based on semi-structured interviews with parents and using the Tall Poppy Syndrome (TPS) and social comparison as sensitizing concepts, the study explores how parents interpret the reactions of their social environment, the emotional costs they report, and how parents and children shape the family language policy (FLP) over time. Both families described scrutiny from relatives, friends and peers, a lack of local support, and growing self-consciousness in public. In both cases, these pressures, together with the children’s own reluctance and school-related difficulties, contributed to easing the original policy. Parents nevertheless viewed their children’s English as a worthwhile outcome. The findings suggest that family agency in NNB is multidirectional and includes adaptation and de-escalation, and that TPS is a useful lens and a sensitizing concept that must be considered alongside monolingual and na-tive-speaker ideologies.
